commentary_summary: The market is moderating after undergoing high utilisation towards the end of December, which is being reflected by a decline in the tonne-miles covered as well as the ballast speed. | The global ballast speed was on average 9.5 knots last week, lower by as much as 1 knot in the period last year. | Additionally, we project a slower start to the year as compared to the last year as congestion levels are much lower YoY in most regions. | The subdued speed as well as congestion will likely provide ample supply stretch in the market, which will weigh down the rates this week.

commentary_title: Handysize tonne-miles index drops amid shifts in grain trade
commentary_summary: Global Handysize utilisation remained stable at 93.3%, following an increase last week. In contrast, the tonne-miles index declined significantly, reaching 87 in week 9, nearly 10% lower YoY. This shift can be attributed to decreased EU grain exports. | Ballast tonnage at anchorage in the Atlantic decreased 2% due to a weak French harvest and competition from cheaper Black Sea grains. Conversely, laden tonnage at anchorage in the Atlantic increased 7.7% WoW, driven by an 8% YoY rise in corn imports into the EU. | Ballast speed decreased 7.7% YoY this week while laden speed declined 1.7% WoW.

The Handysize tonne-mile index experienced a sharp decline in the first two weeks of March. Although it recovered to some extent in the second half of March, it further declined 3%, reaching 91.7 in week 14. | Baltic benchmark rates mirrored this trend, aligning with utilisation patterns. Global laden speed dropped significantly by 3.6%, with ballast speed following the same . | The cross-Atlantic region remained quiet, marked by a substantial decrease in laden tonnage underway. More vessels gathered at ports, contributing to increased congestion at anchor in the Atlantic.

commentary_title: Handysize market weakens as Pacific region remained quiet
commentary_summary: Handysize utilisation started to decline after the conflict between Iran and Israel started last week which also weakened the tonne-mile demand. | The Pacific market remained subdued due to vessel oversupply, which eased congestion of ballasting and laden vessels. Although there was some firm activity in the Atlantic, it was insufficient to offset the overall weakness, and therefore, the market continued to experience headwinds. | However, spot rates on the Europe–South America route surged over the past four weeks, driven by strong demand and robust activity in the Atlantic and USG, creating a more optimistic market outlook in the West. The laden speed in the West also remained elevated throughout this period.

The Handysize tonne-miles index surged 11% QoQ in 3Q25, supported by seasonal firmness. Laden speed increased in accordance. Port congestion also rose 10.8% MoM in the west, reducing the share of vessels underway. | Laden tonnage at anchor increased across both East and West, driving momentum in spot rates, which continued on a strong upward trajectory. | Strength in the Atlantic and Indian Ocean underpinned sentiment, while the Pacific market remained comparatively subdued and positional.

commentary_title: Handysize market strengthens amid rising rates
commentary_summary: Handysize utilisation saw a modest uptick in Week 40, supported by a parallel rise in Baltic benchmark rates. The tonne-miles index also trended higher, with the Handysize segment outperforming other segments, recording a 23% YoY increase. | Vessel capacity at anchor in the East rose 8.9% MoM, driven by a higher share of laden vessels. Spot rates on the China–Southeast Asia route also strengthened, signalling improving market sentiment across the region. | While the Laden congestion in China remained low this week, it saw a sharp increase in India. Meanwhile, ballast tonnage in the Atlantic fell sharply, dropping below 2023 and 2024 levels.

commentary_title: Atlantic softness weighs on Handysize rates as Pacific holds firm
commentary_summary: The tonne-miles index declined slightly by 0.8 percentage points to 117, in tandem with the falling Baltic benchmark HS7TC, which fell 494 points WoW to $16,466/day. In the Atlantic, the US Gulf and South Atlantic lost momentum as more vessel availability and limited fresh enquiries widened the supply-demand imbalance, placing downward pressure on rates. | The Pacific market continued to outperform the Atlantic, supported by sufficient cargo demand to absorb increasing tonnage. Although Australian grain remained limited and Southeast Asia saw a gradual build-up in vessel availability, steady activity in the Far East and continued fresh cargoes from the Indian Ocean helped prevent a sharper contraction. | Market participants continued to monitor Typhoon Bavi for potential supply disruptions across the Pacific. At the same time, growing vessel availability in Southeast Asia suggests that a stronger August cargo will be required to prevent further rate erosion, while improving cargo visibility in the Atlantic will be essential to absorb oversupply and restore market balance.

commentary_title: Handysize rates remain under pressure as tonnage increases across both basins
commentary_summary: The Handysize tonne-miles index edged down 5% to reach 116.2 in week 32, with rates continuing to move differently across both basins. Limited fresh enquiry and an increasing pool of vessel availability kept charterers in control, while the Atlantic saw further weakness in ECSA and softer activity in the US Gulf. The Continent and Mediterranean remained subdued, with only limited scrap and cement-related demand. The speed also slowed down across the east and the west. | The US Gulf faced the sharpest correction as a lack of new cargoes and a growing number of vessels weighed on fronthaul and transatlantic rates. The Continent also softened amid weaker Turkish scrap and fertiliser demand, while the East Mediterranean remained comparatively resilient, supported by new grain cargoes and stronger premiums for owners willing to trade via the Red Sea. | The Pacific lost some momentum as enquiries from North Asia eased and vessel availability increased across Southeast Asia and East Coast India. However, steady Chinese demand for Indonesian coal, continued South African cargoes in the Indian Ocean, and improving Australian export activity helped in limiting the further downside.

commentary_title: Atlantic strength offsets softer Asian sentiments in Handysize market
commentary_summary: The Drewry's Tonne-miles index rose WoW to 119.2, with sentiment turning more positional as September cargoes emerged. The Atlantic led the improvement, particularly ECSA and the US Gulf, while the Continent and Mediterranean remained quiet but showed firmer rates towards the end of the week. The global laden speed also increased in tandem. | The South Atlantic remained the strongest area, supported by continued grain demand and tightening available tonnage. The US Gulf also improved towards the end, with fixtures around $20,000/day for transatlantic business, while stronger demolitions enquiry helped lift sentiment in the Continent and Mediterranean. | The Pacific market started slowly but gained some momentum in the Far East, where a relatively balanced tonnage supported rates. However, Southeast Asia remained subdued, and the Far East continued to face limited cargo availability, keeping charterers in a strong position. Period enquiry remained healthy, with increased interest in employment of up to one year.
